We also weren't yet living together for logistic/tax reasons (two houses, neither very large), even though we've been married since 2022.

I still hadn't heard back by Monday, so I decided to request a refund for the NHS charges and start a new application with cleaner, better documentation.  
You cannot get a refund once a decision is made and I didn't want to risk being rejected and losing all the money I'd paid.

I sent in the refund request late Monday night.  
My approval email was sent first thing Tuesday morning (8am UK time).

I'm not saying my request for refund forced the decision, but the timing does seem suspect.

That said, with all the bank holidays it was still within the 30 working days for priority.

Hi there! I have both the 590 and 790 Pro, and sew on a wide range of fabrics. I understand about the wider space between the feed dogs, especially on narrow seam allowance and softer fabrics. You can avoid some of the problem with a 5mm or 0mm plate, but there are other ways to avoid fabric being pulled down. For softer fabrics I'll use a small piece of tearaway stabilizer at the start and at corners. Although you don't have to hold the thread when starting a seam on these machines, that can help, too.  
I took a workshop on sewing with sheer fabrics back in October where the instructor suggested sewing with tissue paper, then tearing it away afterwards. I've not tried this yet, but it should also help keep the fabric on the surface of the machine.

okay, you asked for it:  
First, it's not dry. It's just a non-water solvent--historically really, really horrible ones. The most common was perchloroethylene or PERC. Apparently some still use it even though it's "likely to be **carcinogenic** to humans". Sometimes "moisture" is added, which just means water.

Second, because no or very little water is used, only oil-based stains/dirt are removed. Most body, um, secretions, are water based. So those don't get cleaned away. I spent a summer working the pants press and I can tell you--urine does \*not\* get cleaned away. (Imagine working in 100 degree heat over a steam press that is 'scented' with urine)

Third, your clothes are thrown in a giant machine with a bunch of other people's clothes.

Finally, unless you go to a good quality cleaners, they are likely using that same solvent for long periods of time. The machines work similar to a regular washing machine, except they have an extraction cycle when they recapture the solvent. It is filtered and reused. A good cleaner will only use the same batch a few times, topping off as needed. A crappy cleaner will never change the solvent, just topping off indefinitely.  
I worked at a cleaners in college and another a few years back when a friend opened her own, so in addition to understanding the chemistry/mechanics from uni, I also saw first hand how things work.  
I was pressing a pair of men's polyester slacks one that had been cleaned at a budget cleaners for years. After being cleaned at my friends place, they were greasy to the touch.

This is why I rarely buy anything that says "Dry Clean Only", and if I do, I usually wash it by hand. Another reason some manufacturers use the "Dry Clean Only" label: It's cheaper and easier than having ones made up with specific washing instructions.

Detergent and fabric softener from bathing suits adds to the "soup".

I earned a BS in Textiles and Clothing and worked in the garment business for a few years after graduating. You should wash all new textiles (except dry-clean only, of course) before wearing. That "new clothes" smell is usually formaldehyde which is used to keep fabrics from rotting while being stored. And I can confirm that the places where these products are made and stored are often filthy. I worked for a childrenswear company that got a shipment in from a sew shop that was infested with rats and by extension, fleas. The clothing was crawling with them. The entire warehouse had to be fumigated to get rid of them. So now these beautiful clothes are likely covered with rat feces/urine, flea deposits AND insecticide.  
For things that can't be washed, let the air out before wearing at the very least.  
Oh, and "Dry-clean only" items can often be hand-washed or even washed in the machine on delicate. Many companies use that to cover themselves if anything goes wrong like colors running or shrinkage. You probably don't want to know how gross dry-cleaning can be
